newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to maintain "useful role" of nuclear energy.
newsitem.headline: EU to maintain "useful role" of nuclear energy.

text.p: The European Commission proposed common principles for Europe's use of nuclear power on Wednesday, saying it was contributing to the EU's energy supply and economic welfare.
"Nuclear energy is today an industrial, economic and social reality," European Union Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis said in a statement.
There are more than 140 nuclear reactors operating in eight of the EU's 15 member states, generating one third of the bloc's electricity and making it the world's leading producer.
However, "to maintain the useful role of nuclear energy in the future" some common EU principles have to be followed, the Commission said.
The Commission adopted at its weekly meeting a draft "Illustrative Nuclear Programme", assessing the different features of EU nuclear energy and identifying its challenges.
The Commission said the use of nuclear energy had a favourable impact on the security of supply, qualified jobs, fuel imports and reductions of carbon dioxide emissions.
Nuclear energy helped to reduce fossil fuel consumption and the subsequent reduced demand on the international oil market had made a contribution towards "moderating" oil prices.
"On the other hand, there are questions related to the concerns on safety, transport, management of waste, decommissioning and non-prolifiration," the Commission said.
Further technological development and increased international cooperation was needed, it said.
The Commission programme did not state production targets, giving priority to the free functioning of the market.
Among the suggested principles, the Commission said each member state had the right to decide whether to develop the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

In addition, member states need "to ensure a high degree of nuclear safety, respect non-proliferation requirements as provided for in relevant international agreements as well as high level of human health production."

The Association of the European Nuclear Industry Forums (FORATOM) welcomed the programme, saying the EU must rely on non-fossil fuel electricity generation if it is to meet its international commitments to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases.
"The realistic economic solution is more reliance on nuclear energy," FORATOM said in a statement.

However, it said the industry acknowledged the challenges it faced. "While progress has been made on programmes for nuclear waste storage facilities and plant decommissioning, public acceptance issues remain," FORATOM said.
